description.summary: Japanese mountain spirits, classed as both yōkai and kami, ranging from lesser bird-like kotengu to high-ranking long-nosed daitengu, originally portrayed as Buddhist demons but later re-imagined as protective mountain guardians and martial-arts mentors.
description.full: Tengu (天狗, literally 'heavenly dog') are legendary creatures of Japanese folklore, classified as both a kind of yōkai (supernatural beings) and as a kind of kami (Shinto deity). They inhabit deep forests and mountains, especially in central and northern Honshu. Two main types are distinguished: kotengu, lesser, more bird-like figures often called karasu-tengu ('crow tengu') or konoha-tengu ('leaf tengu'); and daitengu, the high-ranking, more humanoid 'great tengu' (also yamabushi-tengu, in mountain-ascetic dress) characterized by very long, prominent noses (hanatakatengu). Earlier Japanese sources, especially the late Heian and Kamakura-era Buddhist texts (Konjaku Monogatari, Genpei Jōsuiki), depict tengu as disruptive demons who possess people, abduct monks, and foretell war. From the 14th century onward — exemplified by the legend in which the Daitengu Sōjōbō of Mount Kurama trains Minamoto no Yoshitsune in swordsmanship — they are increasingly re-cast as protective mountain spirits and martial-arts masters. Major named daitengu include Sōjōbō of Mount Kurama, Tarōbō of Mount Atago, and Jirōbō of the Hira Mountains; the 18th-century 'Tengu Meigikō' by Hayashi Razan / Inoue Enryō tradition lists their hierarchy. Tengu are widely venerated at mountain shrines, appear in Noh and kabuki, and remain a strong presence in modern manga, anime, and video games.

etymology.origin: Japanese 天 ('heaven, sky') + 狗 ('dog'), borrowed from Chinese tiāngǒu (天狗), originally a celestial dog associated with meteoric phenomena.
etymology.meaning: Literally 'heavenly dog'; the Japanese figure diverged early from the Chinese original to become a bird-like / humanoid mountain being.
etymology.first_use: Earliest recorded Japanese mention in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE).

related_phenomena.description: Chinese celestial-dog source of the Japanese name

related_phenomena.description: Real-world Japanese mountain ascetics whose dress was adopted in tengu iconography

related_phenomena.name: Yōkai
related_phenomena.description: Wider category of Japanese supernatural beings to which tengu belong

related_phenomena.name: Kami
related_phenomena.description: Shinto deities; daitengu are sometimes worshipped as kami

features.description: The hallmark long red nose of the great tengu, developed in iconography from the 14th century onward
Lesser tengu retain crow- or kite-like beaks, wings, and feathers
Most daitengu wear the costume of a mountain ascetic, including the small black box-shaped tokin
Magical feather fan associated especially with daitengu

physical.morphology: Variable. Lesser tengu are humanoid bird-like beings; greater tengu are tall humanoids with long noses, often with hawk-, kite-, or crow-like wings.

abilities.description: Daitengu and karasu-tengu fly between mountain peaks
Adopt human form, particularly that of wandering monks, to test or deceive humans

abilities.ability: Mastery of swordsmanship and martial arts
abilities.description: Daitengu reputedly train heroes — most famously Minamoto no Yoshitsune by Sōjōbō of Mount Kurama
Tengu use the hauchiwa to raise winds and storms
Older Buddhist sources describe tengu abducting and possessing monks and children

habitat_preference: specific sacred mountains (Kurama, Atago, Hira, Hiei)
patterns: Strongly territorial — each named daitengu is bound to a specific mountain
Test the pride and discipline of monks, swordsmen, and travellers
Reward the humble and disciplined, punish the proud and arrogant
Associated with sudden mountain weather and 'tengu pranks' (kamikakushi)

range.description: Tengu are exclusively associated with Japan and concentrated in the country's mountainous interior, especially central Honshu.
regions: Kansai (Mount Kurama, Mount Atago, Mount Hiei)

hotspots.name: Mount Kurama (Kibune-Kurama, Kyoto)

location.description: Mountain north of Kyoto; traditional home of the daitengu Sōjōbō

hotspots.notes: Site of Kurama-dera and the Yoshitsune-Sōjōbō tradition.

hotspots.name: Mount Atago (Kyoto)

location.description: Mountain west of Kyoto; traditional seat of the daitengu Tarōbō

hotspots.notes: Atago Shrine is associated with fire prevention and the daitengu Tarōbō.

hotspots.name: Mount Takao (Tokyo)

location.description: Mountain west of Tokyo; major modern site of tengu veneration at Yakuō-in temple

hotspots.notes: Famous tengu statues mark the approach to Yakuō-in.

peak_activity_periods.description: Buddhist 'demon-tengu' literature: Konjaku Monogatari, Genpei Jōsuiki
Re-imagining of tengu as martial mentors and mountain guardians; Yoshitsune cycle
Hierarchies of named daitengu codified (Tengu Meigikō tradition); widespread woodblock-print imagery

origins.cultural_roots: Tengu emerge from the meeting of Chinese tiāngǒu lore, Indigenous Japanese mountain-spirit (yama-no-kami) tradition, and the practices of Japanese Buddhism (especially Shugendō and the yamabushi).
origins.earliest_accounts: First Japanese mention in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), which describes a mysterious sky-creature interpreted as a tengu.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Shugendō mountain asceticism, to Buddhist demon traditions, and to Shinto kami of specific mountains.

timeline.event: Nihon Shoki records the first mention of a 'tengu' in Japanese sources, identifying a meteoric or aerial phenomenon
timeline.significance: Earliest written use of the term in Japan

timeline.event: Konjaku Monogatari-shū (late Heian) presents tengu as Buddhist demons who possess priests and abduct monks
Genpei Jōsuiki and other late-Kamakura/Nanboku-chō works describe a hierarchical tengu society with named daitengu
Tengu of Mount Kurama (Sōjōbō) is firmly established in the Yoshitsune legend cycle as a martial mentor
Hayashi Razan / Inoue Enryō traditions and the 'Tengu Meigikō' rank major daitengu by mountain
timeline.significance: Codifies the named-daitengu hierarchy still cited today

history.modern_era: Tengu remain prominent in Japanese religious practice (mountain shrines, tengu festivals such as Hachiōji Yakuō-in's Hi-watari and the Kurama Hi-matsuri), in Noh and kabuki repertoire, and in modern popular media (manga, anime, video games such as Touhou Project, Nioh, and Onmyōji).

documentary.name: Nihon Shoki (720 CE)
documentary.description: Earliest extant Japanese text recording the term 'tengu', applied to a celestial / meteoric phenomenon.
documentary.analysis: Primary source for the date of the term's introduction in Japanese sources.

documentary.name: Konjaku Monogatari-shū (late Heian)
documentary.description: Buddhist tale collection portraying tengu as demons that abduct and possess monks.
documentary.analysis: Foundational late-Heian witness for the 'demon-tengu' phase.

documentary.name: Tengu Meigikō
documentary.description: Edo-period text ranking the major named daitengu by mountain.
documentary.analysis: Canonical source for the daitengu hierarchy.

scientific.name: Composite cultural construct
scientific.description: Modern Japanese folklorists (Komatsu Kazuhiko and others) treat tengu as a layered figure formed by the integration of Chinese tiāngǒu lore, Indigenous Japanese mountain-spirit traditions, and Buddhist demonology, refracted through Shugendō practice.
evidence_cited: Comparative textual evidence from Nihon Shoki, Konjaku Monogatari, and Genpei Jōsuiki
Iconographic development from Heian to Edo period

stories: Sōjōbō of Mount Kurama trains Minamoto no Yoshitsune in swordsmanship
Konjaku Monogatari tales of tengu possessing monks
Tengu Meigikō hierarchy of named daitengu
folklore.beliefs: Tengu are venerated at numerous mountain shrines and temples; major festivals such as the Kurama Fire Festival and the Hi-watari at Mount Takao acknowledge tengu as guardians of the mountain.

indigenous.significance: Tengu remain part of living Japanese religious culture, intersecting Shugendō, Shinto, and Buddhist practice.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Engage with tengu material in religious and academic Japanese sources rather than treating them only as folkloric curiosities.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: When citing specific shrines and festivals, defer to the relevant temple/shrine documentation.

Edo-period otogizōshi and kibyōshi featuring tengu

Nioh (2017) and Nioh 2 (2020) — tengu enemies and lore
